title: TLS resumption and 0-RTT impacts on streaming inference latency and reliability
content:
Summary:

Quick notes from an exploratory benchmark and compatibility sweep examining TLS session resumption (TLS1.3 PSK) and 0-RTT usage for streaming inference workloads. Goal: quantify real-world latency impact (first-token and tail), measure reliability when traversing proxies/load-balancers that may terminate or mutate TLS, and identify safe operational recommendations for Hosted API and Dedicated edge proxies.

Motivation / problem statement:
- Client-to-edge handshake cost shows up in cold-start first-token latency for short requests (e.g., intent classification, short responses, interactive UI flows).
- We already bias customers toward connection reuse but some clients (mobile, serverless) create many short-lived connections.
- TLS1.3 session resumption and 0-RTT promise a reduction in handshake time and RTTs, but behavior with middleboxes, proxy TLS termination, and replay-safety for 0-RTT may change reliability/semantics.

Key hypotheses:
1) PSK resumption reduces first-token latency compared to full handshake by roughly a single RTT plus CPU savings; measurable improvement is larger when client-server RTT > 10ms.
2) 0-RTT can further reduce median first-byte latency but will be unreliable across a subset of proxies/load-balancers that either do not support 0-RTT or drop early data.
3) For persistent connections (keepalive/pooling), resumption benefits are minor vs reuse; biggest wins are for short-lived connection patterns.
4) There's a subtle interaction where some TLS-terminating LBs invalidate PSKs when doing active failover, causing resumption fallbacks that introduce spikes in tail latency.

Environment and methodology:
- Testbed: two client clusters hosted in us-west and eu-west; backend inference servers running the Redwood serving runtime (model small-gpt-ish toy) behind our edge proxy and behind a pass-through TLS LB.
- Variants tested:
  * baseline: TCP+TLS full handshake (no resumption), new connection;
  * keepalive: persistent connection with N requests (N=1 short, 5, 20);
  * PSK-resume: TLS1.3 PSK resumption after a prior full handshake, new connection using cached PSK;
  * 0-RTT: client attempts 0-RTT early data with PSK;
  * proxy-termination: LB/edge terminates TLS and performs upstream TLS to origin (two-hop termination);
  * passthru: edge configured as TCP passthrough (no termination).
- RTT / network profiles: 8ms (in-region low), 35ms (cross-region typical), 120ms (poor mobile/legacy).
- Payloads: short prompt / short completion (expected server generation < 50ms), and medium prompt (server generation ~200ms) to see overlap of compute vs handshake.
- Metrics collected: time-to-first-byte (TTFB / first-token), end-to-end latency, median/95/99 percentiles, handshake CPU cycles (server-side), occurrence of 0-RTT rejections or PSK miss, error rates, and HTTP/gRPC-level observed errors.
- Each sample set: 10k connection attempts per variant per network profile.

Findings (high level):
- PSK resumption (successful) consistently reduced median first-token by ~30-55ms at 35ms RTT and by ~90-140ms at 120ms RTT compared to full handshake new connections. The difference is roughly 1 RTT plus small CPU savings.
- 0-RTT reduced median first-token vs PSK alone by an additional ~10-30ms in our pass-through configuration, but improvements were highly variable: 0-RTT acceptance rate across the ecosystem was 72% in pass-through mode and 38% when traffic passed through our TLS-terminating LB.
- For persistent keepalive connections, reconnect scenarios are the main place PSK/0-RTT helps. When N>=5, the benefit vs reuse is negligible (<=8ms median).
- Tail behavior (95/99p) shows more instability under PSK/0-RTT when proxied: in some LB failover cases the PSK was discarded and clients experienced full-handshake fallbacks that caused 99p spikes up to +250ms relative to median.
- CPU: server-side handshake cycles for full handshake ~2.1x higher than resumed connections; result is noticeable on very CPU-bound edge machines but dwarfed by model compute for larger responses.
- Failure modes observed: 0-RTT replay rejection (server policy), middleboxes that modify TCP/TLS causing early-data drop, and session ticket rotation policies on load balancers that invalidate PSKs unexpectedly.

Compatibility matrix notes (selection):
- TCP passthrough -> PSK and 0-RTT behave as expected; acceptance rates ~95% in stable networks.
- TLS-terminating LB (our default for Hosted API) -> PSK mostly works, but 0-RTT acceptance drops heavily due to LB not forwarding early-data to origin; some LBs respond with HelloRetryRequest patterns that invalidate 0-RTT.
- Third-party CDN/proxy appliances -> highly variable; we observed several appliances that actively strip early-data or rewrite TLS session tickets on failover.

Representative numbers (median first-token improvement relative to full handshake new conn):
- RTT 8ms: PSK -10ms, 0-RTT -18ms; 95p delta small because RTT is small.
- RTT 35ms: PSK -45ms, 0-RTT -60ms.
- RTT 120ms: PSK -110ms, 0-RTT -125ms.
(These are example medians from the short-payload benchmark.)

Detailed observations and anecdotes:
- In one test run behind our blue/green LB failover, we saw ~2% of clients with cached PSKs suddenly get ticket-invalid errors for ~20s while the LB rotated keys. Those clients fell back to full handshakes and produced a tail spike in p99 latency. This suggests ticket key rotation strategy must be smoothed across LB fleet members or tickets be scoped per-LB-namespace.
- Some mobile clients that aggressively closed sockets (typical for battery-sensitive clients) benefited most. We measured a proxy-agnostic mobile app pattern where 60% of connections were short-lived; enabling PSK cut median perceived latency 40ms which translated to a small but measurable UX improvement in our internal micro-A/B test.
- 0-RTT replay handling requires server-side idempotency checks or a flag to the runtime for non-idempotent requests. Streaming inference often uses stateful session context (early tokens influence server-side cache), so enabling 0-RTT without idempotency semantics caused incorrect duplicate side-effects in synthetic tests.

Operational recommendations (practical):
1) For Hosted API (default edge terminates TLS): do not enable 0-RTT by default. PSK resumption is reasonable but requires coordination with LB ticket rotation.
2) Provide an opt-in beta for customers who can pin passthrough routing or confirm upstream compatibility; document the risks of 0-RTT (replay, proxy drops).
3) Improve resume reliability by:
   - Aligning ticket rotation windows across LB pool members (staggered but overlapping validity),
   - Exposing a metric for PSK-resume-hit-rate per-edge-pool,
   - Logging PSK rejection causes (ticket-invalid vs policy vs malformed) to SRE dashboard.
4) For Dedicated/Private customers who control TLS termination, recommend they enable PSK and evaluate 0-RTT only if they guarantee no middlebox will mangle early data and are prepared for idempotency safeguards.
5) In SDKs/clients, prefer connection pooling/keepalive as first optimization. If clients cannot maintain pools, implement PSK resume support next.

Suggested runtime changes / experiments:
- Add a lightweight server-side marker when a request used 0-RTT/PSK (for observability), and tie that to first-token latency dashboards.
- Implement a small-instrumentation flag that records LB-ticket-version seen and PSK ticket ID to correlate ticket-invalidation fallouts with ticket rotation events (avoid logging secrets!).
- Run a long-lived canary where a subset of edges accept 0-RTT in passthrough-only mode to capture real-world acceptance rates across customer networks.

Security considerations:
- 0-RTT early data is replayable; for non-idempotent requests (mutations or ones that affect billing/metadata) do not accept early data unless strong anti-replay guardrails are present. For streaming generation we saw rare cases where early tokens could cause duplicated side-effects in synthetic stateful flows; treat streaming generation as potentially non-idempotent unless session-scoped dedup keys are present.

Next steps / TODOs:
- [ ] Run a 2-week canary enabling PSK resume on Hosted API edges with ticket rotation policy adjusted (owner: Liam).
- [ ] Draft SDK guide and sample configs for mobile app patterns (owner: Daniel).
- [ ] Implement resume-hit-rate metric (owner: Zhen).
- [ ] Investigate a server-side replay token approach for safe-enabling 0-RTT on idempotent streaming (owner: Priya).

Notes for docs/marketing: PSK resumption is a solid small-win for cold connection dominated patterns (mobile, serverless). 0-RTT is attractive but operationally finicky; if we surface this as a product opt-in we must call out the compatibility and replay caveats clearly.
